cards.definition: An IAM identity with permissions that any trusted principal can assume to get temporary credentials, instead of long-term keys.
An AWS Organizations policy that sets the maximum permissions available to accounts; it never grants permissions itself.
An IAM managed policy set on a user or role that defines the maximum permissions that identity-based policies can grant it.
AWS Security Token Service, which issues temporary, limited-privilege credentials for roles and federated users.
Service for workforce single sign-on and centrally managed access to multiple AWS accounts and applications.
A user directory in Amazon Cognito that handles sign-up and sign-in for app users and issues tokens.
Exchanges authenticated or guest identities for temporary AWS credentials mapped to IAM roles.
Identifies resources shared with external principals and helps validate and generate least-privilege policies.
A stateful virtual firewall at the instance or network interface level that has allow rules only.
A stateless subnet-level firewall with numbered allow and deny rules for inbound and outbound traffic.
A route-table target that privately connects a VPC to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB at no additional charge.
A web application firewall that filters HTTP and HTTPS requests to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, and other resources.
Managed DDoS protection; Standard is automatic at no extra charge, and Advanced is a paid subscription for higher levels of protection.
Threat detection service that analyzes CloudTrail events, VPC flow logs, and DNS logs for malicious activity.
Stores and retrieves secrets such as database credentials and can rotate them automatically.
Managed service for creating and controlling cryptographic keys used to protect data across AWS services.
Write-once-read-many protection for S3 object versions, with governance and compliance retention modes.
Uses machine learning and pattern matching to discover and report sensitive data in Amazon S3.
A managed queue that buffers messages between producers and consumers so they scale and fail independently. Consumers pull messages.
The period after a consumer receives an SQS message during which other consumers cannot see it. Set it longer than the processing time.
An SQS queue that receives messages that exceeded the maximum receive count on the source queue, so failures can be inspected.
Receiving SQS messages with a wait time greater than zero so the call waits for messages, reducing empty responses and cost.
Publishing one message to an SNS topic that delivers it to many subscribers, commonly one SQS queue per consumer.
A serverless event bus that routes events from AWS services, applications and SaaS partners to targets using rules.
A serverless workflow service that orchestrates services as state machines with retries, error handling and branching.
A managed database proxy that pools and shares connections, protecting databases from connection exhaustion by bursty clients such as Lambda.
An RDS deployment with a synchronous standby in another AZ for automatic failover. It is for availability, not read scaling.
An asynchronously replicated copy of a database used to scale read traffic and, for cross-Region replicas, to support disaster recovery.
An Aurora database spanning multiple Regions with storage-level replication, low replication lag and fast cross-Region failover.
A multi-Region, multi-active replication feature where each replica table accepts reads and writes.
Recovery time objective is how long a workload may be down; recovery point objective is how much data loss, measured in time, is acceptable.
A disaster recovery strategy that keeps core components such as replicated data ready, with compute scaled up only during a disaster.
A service that provides static anycast IP addresses and routes traffic to healthy Regional endpoints without depending on DNS caching.
EBS volume type for latency-sensitive workloads that need sustained, high IOPS, such as large databases.
General Purpose SSD EBS volume with a baseline of 3,000 IOPS where IOPS and throughput can be provisioned independently of size.
Temporary block storage physically attached to the host; very fast but data is lost when the instance stops, hibernates or terminates.
Managed, elastic NFS file system that many Linux instances across Availability Zones can mount at the same time.
High-performance file system for HPC and machine learning workloads that can be linked to an S3 bucket.
Feature that speeds long-distance transfers to S3 by routing uploads through CloudFront edge locations.
Packs EC2 instances close together in one AZ for low-latency, high-throughput networking.
Auto Scaling policy that adjusts capacity to keep a metric near a target value.
Lambda setting that keeps a set number of execution environments initialized to avoid cold starts.
Serverless compute engine for containers on ECS and EKS, with no instances to manage.
Asynchronously replicated copy of a database used to scale read traffic.
Fully managed in-memory cache for DynamoDB that delivers microsecond read latency.
Managed database proxy that pools and shares connections to reduce connection exhaustion.
Service giving static anycast IP addresses that route TCP and UDP traffic over the AWS global network to optimal endpoints.
Managed service that loads streaming data into S3, Redshift, OpenSearch and other destinations with no consumer code.
An S3 storage class that automatically moves objects between access tiers as access patterns change, with no retrieval fees and a small per-object monitoring fee.
A configuration that transitions objects between storage classes or expires them after a set time, and can also remove noncurrent versions and incomplete multipart uploads.
The lowest-cost S3 storage class, meant for long-term archives that are rarely read and can wait hours for retrieval.
A general purpose SSD volume type priced about 20 percent lower per GiB than gp2, where you can provision IOPS and throughput independently of size.
An EC2 instance that uses spare capacity at a large discount and can be interrupted by AWS with a two-minute notice, suited to fault-tolerant work.
A pricing model that gives a lower rate in exchange for a commitment to a consistent amount of usage per hour for one or three years.
A service that analyzes utilization metrics and recommends right-sized EC2 instances, Auto Scaling groups, EBS volumes and Lambda functions.
An Aurora configuration that scales database capacity up and down in fine increments with load, so you pay for the capacity used.
An RDS billing commitment for a one or three year term that lowers the hourly rate for databases that run steadily.
A capacity mode where DynamoDB bills per read and write request with no capacity planning, suited to unpredictable traffic.
A route table target that privately connects a VPC to S3 or DynamoDB at no additional charge, avoiding NAT gateway data processing fees.
A NAT gateway bills for each hour it runs and for each GB of data it processes, so heavy traffic to AWS services is often cheaper through VPC endpoints.
